documents.unit: Digital Futures Institute (TC AI and Pedagogy Working Group)
documents.title: TC Guidance: Developing a Generative AI Policy for Your Course
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule of its own: it says "TC encourages instructors to consider how generative AI can be integrated" and offers "five examples of syllabi statements reflecting varied stances" to "use and adapt as you see fit". The decision is handed to instructors and the examples are tiers.
tiers: Permitted in Some Cases: Refer to Individual Assignments
Permitted in Some Cases: For Specific Purposes
Permitted in Some Cases: Confer with Instructor Prior to Use
Generally Permitted with Attribution or Disclosure
documents.summary: Guidance from the Digital Futures Institute that tells instructors to set and clearly communicate their own generative AI policy, weighing learning goals, equity, privacy and copyright. It supplies five adaptable syllabus statements from a full ban to open use with disclosure.

units.why: The opening sentence urges instructors to consider integrating AI into courses ('TC encourages instructors to consider how generative AI can be integrated'). It is an institutional encouragement aimed at instructors, so actor is instructor and modality should. P02 is the nearest type but fits only partly because it encourages consideration, not student use itself.
units.anchor: TC encourages instructors to consider how generative AI can be integrated into courses
units.policy: TC encourages instructors to consider how generative AI can be integrated into courses.
units.fit_note: Encourages instructors to consider integrating AI; it does not itself permit or require student use.

units.why: It tells instructors to be 'explicit and transparent in communicating this policy to students' in the syllabus, in class and on assignments. That is a duty to state AI expectations, so P09; P66 (explaining the rules) is not chosen because the sentence is about stating them, not justifying them.
units.anchor: be explicit and transparent in communicating this policy to students
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to be explicit and transparent in communicating their generative AI policy to students in the syllabus, in class, and whenever relevant to assignments.

units.why: The first factor listed for policy design is 'Alignment with learning goals'. It ties AI decisions to learning objectives, which is P83.
units.anchor: Alignment with learning goals
units.policy: In devising a generative AI policy, instructors should take alignment with learning goals into account.

units.why: The second factor is 'Equity and access for all students'. It names equity as a design consideration, which fits P51 (equity and access).
units.anchor: Equity and access for all students
units.frag_start: Equity and access for all students
units.frag_end: Equity and access for all students
units.policy: In devising a generative AI policy, instructors should take equity and access for all students into account.

units.why: The third factor is 'Information security and data privacy'. It asks instructors to weigh privacy in policy design. P50 is the nearest type but only partly fits, since no one is told to protect data or prefer vetted tools.
units.anchor: Information security and data privacy
units.policy: In devising a generative AI policy, instructors should take information security and data privacy into account.
units.fit_note: Only a factor for instructors to weigh; it does not tell anyone to protect data or use vetted tools.

units.why: The fourth factor, 'Copyright and academic integrity', pairs two concerns. I chose P52 because copyright has no other mention in the document, while integrity is handled by the example statements under P36. P52 fits only partly.
units.anchor: Copyright and academic integrity
units.policy: In devising a generative AI policy, instructors should take copyright and academic integrity into account.
units.fit_note: Pairs copyright with academic integrity as one factor to weigh; only the copyright half is the type.

units.why: The page offers five syllabus statements 'reflecting varied stances' for instructors to 'use and adapt as you see fit'. That is a menu of named tiers from no AI to open use (P05). P04 is not chosen because the point of the unit is the set of tiers, not who decides.
units.anchor: five examples of syllabi statements reflecting varied stances on using AI in courses
units.policy: The guidance provides five example syllabus statements reflecting varied stances on using AI in courses, which instructors may use and adapt as they see fit.

units.why: Example 1 says 'Students are prohibited from using generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to complete coursework or assignments'. A course-wide ban on AI for coursework is P01 and the unit stance is prohibit.
units.anchor: Students are prohibited from using generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to complete coursework

units.why: Example 1 says a violation 'will be considered academic dishonesty' and handled under the syllabus and College integrity procedures. This classifies AI misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Violation of this policy will be considered academic dishonesty

units.why: Example 1 offers an accommodation route: students registered with OASID with a 'generative AI accommodation' should speak to the instructor. P51 covers accommodations; I chose it over P97 because the sentence is about getting an accommodation, not about accessibility of AI output. The same sentence recurs in Examples 2, 4 and 5 and is coded once.
units.anchor: registered with OASID with a generative AI accommodation, please speak with me directly
units.frag_start: If you are a student registered
units.policy: Students registered with OASID with a generative AI accommodation should speak with the instructor directly about their needs.
units.fit_note: About disability accommodations; the type is mainly about cost and equal access.

units.why: Example 2 says 'Each assignment will specify whether AI can be used and, if so, how it should be employed.' Permission is decided per assignment, so P04.
units.anchor: Each assignment will specify whether AI can be used and, if so
units.policy: Each assignment will specify whether AI can be used and, if so, how it should be employed.

units.why: Example 2 says students 'may use generative AI tools for certain assignments where indicated', so AI is allowed only where an assignment says so. That is a narrow permission set per assignment: P04, unit stance restrict.
units.anchor: Students may use generative AI tools for certain assignments where indicated.

units.why: 'It is the student's responsibility to carefully read and follow these guidelines' puts on the student the duty to learn each assignment's AI rule, which is P78.
units.anchor: to carefully read and follow these guidelines
units.policy: It is the student's responsibility to carefully read and follow each assignment's guidelines on AI use.

units.why: Example 2 requires 'citations or disclosure detailing the specific AI tools and models used'. It requires disclosure and names tool and model but not prompt or output, so P25 fits partly; P24 is more general. The same sentence recurs in Examples 4 and 5.
units.anchor: Students must include citations or disclosure detailing the specific AI tools and models used.
units.fit_note: Names tools and models only, not prompts or outputs.

units.why: Example 2 says 'Unauthorized use will be considered academic dishonesty'. Use beyond what an assignment allows is treated as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Unauthorized use will be considered academic dishonesty

units.why: Example 3 lists as a permitted use 'generating summaries or explanations of challenging material for your own reflection'. That is AI explaining and summarizing material for understanding (P12). The text is a fill-in template for instructors.
units.anchor: generating summaries or explanations of challenging material for your own reflection
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI tools
units.policy: Generative AI tools may be used for generating summaries or explanations of challenging material for the student's own reflection.

units.why: Example 3 lists 'helping you find background information about a topic' as a permitted use. This is AI as a search or background aid, closest to P12.
units.anchor: helping you find background information about a topic
units.policy: Generative AI tools may be used for helping to find background information about a topic.
units.fit_note: Background research on a topic rather than understanding course concepts.

units.why: Example 3 permits 'drafting outlines to help you organize your thoughts'. I chose P15 (idea generation, exploring approaches) over P91 (editing writing) because the use is organizing thoughts before writing, not revising text.
units.anchor: drafting outlines to help you organize your thoughts
units.policy: Generative AI tools may be used for drafting outlines to help organize one's thoughts.
units.fit_note: Outlining to organize thoughts, which is only loosely brainstorming.

units.why: Example 3 permits 'helping to improve grammar and style', which is editing support for writing (P91).
units.anchor: helping to improve grammar and style
units.policy: Generative AI tools may be used for helping to improve grammar and style.

units.why: Example 3 says AI 'may NOT be used for any other purposes' than the listed ones: a closed list with everything else banned. No type for closed lists exists and P05 covers tiers only, so this is a fit with a note, not P01 because AI is allowed for listed uses.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools may NOT be used for any other purposes
units.frag_start: Generative AI tools may NOT be
units.policy: Generative AI tools may not be used for any purposes other than those listed as permitted.
units.fit_note: A closed list of permitted uses with everything else banned; the type is about named tiers.

units.why: The template slot 'you may not use AI to [specific prohibited uses, e.g. draft writing assignments, analyze data, etc]' asks the instructor to name banned uses, with drafting writing and analyzing data as examples. Drafting submitted writing is P19.
units.anchor: you may not use AI to
units.frag_start: and you may not use AI to
units.policy: Students may not use AI for specific prohibited uses named by the instructor, for example to draft writing assignments or analyze data.
units.fit_note: A template slot for instructor-chosen prohibited uses; examples are drafting writing and analyzing data.

units.why: Example 3 says permitted tasks must 'include citations or disclosure detailing the specific AI tools and models used and how they were used'. Tool, model and manner of use are required, so P25.
units.anchor: disclosure detailing the specific AI tools and models used and how they were used
units.frag_start: AI tools in this course are

units.why: Example 4 allows AI 'only after obtaining explicit approval from the instructor'. The default is no AI unless the instructor approves, case by case, so P04 with unit stance restrict.
units.anchor: only after obtaining explicit approval from the instructor
units.frag_start: Students are allowed to use generative
units.policy: Students are allowed to use generative AI tools in their coursework only after obtaining explicit approval from the instructor.

units.why: Example 4 requires students to 'submit, in writing, a brief proposal' on how and why they will use the tool before using it. P10 (ask before using) is nearest, but this is a mandatory written proposal, so a fit note is added.
units.anchor: students must submit, in writing, a brief proposal outlining how the generative AI
units.policy: Before using any generative AI technology, students must submit in writing a brief proposal outlining how the tool will be used and its purpose in the context of the assignment.
units.fit_note: A mandatory written proposal before use, not only asking when unsure.

units.why: 'Approval will be granted based on the appropriateness and educational value of the proposed use' states the criteria the instructor applies. P83 (tie AI decisions to learning aims) is the nearest, but the criterion is educational value, so a fit note is added.
units.anchor: Approval will be granted based on the appropriateness and educational value
units.frag_start: Approval will be granted based on
units.fit_note: States approval criteria (appropriateness and educational value) rather than alignment with stated objectives.

units.why: Example 4 repeats the disclosure duty for approved use ('citations or disclosure detailing the specific AI tools and models used'). Coded under P25 as in Example 2; it is a separate statement inside a different tier.
units.anchor: Students must include citations or disclosure detailing the specific AI tools and models used.
units.fit_note: Names tools and models only, not prompts or outputs.

units.why: Example 4 says unauthorized use, meaning use without approval, is academic dishonesty. It classifies AI misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Unauthorized use will be considered academic dishonesty

units.why: Example 5 says AI is 'generally permitted in this course for research and completion of assignments' if attributed. A permissive default with a disclosure condition is P02.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools are generally permitted in this course for research and completion of assignments
units.frag_start: Generative AI tools are generally permitted
units.policy: Generative AI tools are generally permitted in this course for research and completion of assignments, provided that all AI-generated content is clearly attributed as such in the student's work.

units.why: Example 5 requires AI-generated content to be 'clearly attributed as such in the student's work'. This requires disclosure with the submission, marking AI content (P24).
units.anchor: all AI-generated content is clearly attributed as such

units.why: Example 5 repeats that students must cite or disclose tools and models, so P25 as in Examples 2 and 4, here within the permissive tier.
units.anchor: Students must include citations or disclosure detailing the specific AI tools and models used.
units.fit_note: Names tools and models only, not prompts or outputs.

units.why: Example 5 says 'Failure to properly attribute AI-assisted work will be considered academic dishonesty'. Here nondisclosure itself is the violation, which is P28.
units.anchor: Failure to properly attribute AI-assisted work will be considered academic dishonesty

notes: Units inside Examples 1-5 are coded as the policy each template statement would impose if an instructor adopted it; unit_stance reflects that tier. Sentences repeated across examples (disclosure, academic dishonesty) are coded in each example because they belong to different tiers; the accommodation sentence appears in Examples 1, 2, 4 and 5 and is coded once.
